anomaly_def.Name: Database Memory Allocation Anomaly + Data Block and Index Integrity Anomaly + Storage I/O Throughput Anomaly
anomaly_def.Description:
Database Memory Allocation Anomaly: Excessive or uncontrolled growth of buffer caches, work areas, plan caches, and other engine memory regions that pushes the database process beyond the safe physical-memory or swap envelope of the host. 
Data Block and Index Integrity Anomaly: Physical corruption or logical inconsistency inside data pages and index structures that breaks key ordering, page links, or checksums, making persisted structures unreliable. 
Storage I/O Throughput Anomaly: Sustained read/write demand that exhausts the throughput, IOPS, or latency headroom of the underlying storage subsystem, causing long device queues and elevated I/O wait times.

Composite-anomaly phenomena: When all three root causes manifest concurrently, the system shows a multi-layer failure pattern. Memory pressure drives aggressive paging and frees dirty buffers that must be flushed through a storage layer that is already saturated, elongating checkpoint, redo, and temp-space I/O times. While these writes grind, on-disk corruptions surface or worsen, leading to checksum errors, torn pages, or broken indexes; subsequent retries intensify I/O load and force more memory churn as damaged pages are evicted and reread. The workload experiences sharp spikes in latency, erratic query results (missing or duplicated rows), sudden plan shifts to full scans, frequent lockups due to stalled buffer-pool latches, and possible instance crashes or node evictions triggered by out-of-memory or unrecoverable corruption events. Troubleshooting is complicated because symptoms oscillate between memory exhaustion, I/O saturation, and data-integrity faults, masking their intertwined origins.

Causal interaction: Excessive memory allocation increases dirty-page volume and checkpoint intensity; when the storage subsystem is already throughput-bound, these spikes prolong write-back duration, leaving pages unflushed and heightening vulnerability to power loss or crash scenarios that seed further data and index corruption. Emerging corruption, in turn, provokes repeated read retries, page repairs, or forced table/index rebuilds that generate additional random I/O, aggravating the existing storage bottleneck. Corruption-related cache invalidations and error handling flush large swaths of buffers, recycling memory and amplifying allocation churn, which can reignite memory pressure and OOM risks. The feedback loop among memory over-commitment, constrained I/O bandwidth, and structural corruption accelerates degradation, ultimately threatening availability and data safety across both transactional and analytical workloads.

entry.official_definition: Specifies the number of TCP keepalive messages that can be lost before the server connection to the client is considered dead.
entry.trigger_condition: The number of lost TCP keepalive probes reaches tcp_keepalives_count on systems supporting TCP_KEEPCNT.
entry.workload_impact: The server can consider the client connection dead after the configured keepalive failure threshold.
entry.default_behavior: Default value is 0, selecting the operating system default.
entry.cause_analysis: This timeout is usually triggered when connection establishment, authentication exchange, or session activity does not progress within the allowed time budget.
entry.solution_guidance: Check connection lifecycle, client responsiveness, authentication latency, idle-session handling, and whether connection pools are holding stale sessions.
